title: Laws of Combination of Capacitors
short_intro: Capacitors are combined in series and parallel configurations to achieve desired equivalent capacitance values in electrostatic and alternating current circuits. The total charge stored or equivalent potential drop governs these analytical combinations based on Gauss's law and charge conservation.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of equivalent capacitance for simple series and parallel networks, charge and potential distribution across identical and non-identical capacitors, and energy stored in combined systems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Infinite ladder networks, symmetric bridge circuits, dielectric insertion between capacitor plates in combination, and transient charge redistribution upon switching.

prerequisites: Gauss's law and electric field between parallel plates
Conservation of charge in closed systems

concept_notes.heading: Series Combination of Capacitors
bullets: In a series combination, the same magnitude of charge (Q) resides on the plates of each capacitor due to electrostatic induction.
The total applied potential difference (V) is the sum of potential drops across individual capacitors: V = V&sub1; + V&sub2; + V&sub3; + ...
The reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance equals the sum of the reciprocals of individual capacitances.

concept_notes.heading: Parallel Combination of Capacitors
bullets: In a parallel combination, the potential difference (V) across each capacitor is identical and equal to the applied external voltage.
The total charge (Q) supplied by the source is distributed among the capacitors: Q = Q&sub1; + Q&sub2; + Q&sub3; + ...
The equivalent capacitance is the direct algebraic sum of the individual capacitances, increasing the overall charge storage capacity.

concept_notes.heading: Energy Stored in Capacitor Combinations
bullets: The total electrostatic potential energy stored in either series or parallel combinations is the scalar sum of energies of individual capacitors: U = ∑ U&subi;.
Energy is conserved in ideal combinations, but redistribution between capacitors with different initial potentials results in thermal dissipation and radiative loss.
In series combinations, smaller capacitors bear larger potential drops and consequently store more electrostatic energy (U = Q²/2C).

concept_notes.heading: Complex and Infinite Networks
bullets: Symmetrical ladder networks are analyzed by identifying repeating unit cells and applying recursive algebraic substitutions for equivalent capacitance.
Wheatstone bridge configurations of capacitors reduce to simple series-parallel forms when balanced (C&sub1;/C&sub2; = C&sub3;/C&sub4;).
Dielectric slabs inserted partially into capacitor combinations alter the capacitance values depending on whether the partial regions act in series or parallel.

derivations.title: Equivalent Capacitance of Series Combination
derivations.conditions: n capacitors connected end-to-end across a DC voltage source V
steps: Let capacitors C&sub1;, C&sub2;, ..., C&subn; be connected in series, carrying equal charge Q.
Express the potential difference across each capacitor as V&sub1; = Q/C&sub1;, V&sub2; = Q/C&sub2;, etc.
Write the total potential V = V&sub1; + V&sub2; + ... + V&subn; = Q(1/C&sub1; + 1/C&sub2; + ... + 1/C&subn;).
Define equivalent capacitance C&subs; such that V = Q/C&subs;.

derivations.title: Equivalent Capacitance of Parallel Combination
derivations.conditions: n capacitors connected between two common nodes across voltage V
steps: Let capacitors C&sub1;, C&sub2;, ..., C&subn; be connected in parallel across a common potential V.
The charge on each capacitor is given by Q&sub1; = C&sub1;V, Q&sub2; = C&sub2;V, etc.
The total charge supplied is Q = Q&sub1; + Q&sub2; + ... + Q&subn; = V(C&sub1; + C&sub2; + ... + C&subn;).
Define equivalent capacitance C&subp; such that Q = C&subp;V.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Charge vs Potential Characteristic of Series vs Parallel
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Linear Q-V plots where the slope represents equivalent capacitance (C = Q/V). Parallel combination shows a steeper slope than individual capacitors, while series shows a shallower slope.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: A steeper slope indicates higher capacitance, meaning greater charge stored per unit potential difference.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting slope comparisons in multi-capacitor graphical questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Transient Charging Current Decay in RC Series Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Exponential decay curve of current i(t) = (V/R)exp(-t/RC) against time t.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the time-dependent accumulation of charge on a capacitor combination until steady state (infinite resistance to DC) is reached.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions on time constants (τ = R C&subeq;) for combined capacitor networks.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Bridge Balance Detection Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of a four-capacitor AC bridge circuit driven by an oscillator, with a null detector (earphone or galvanometer) across the bridge diagonal.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: When C&sub1;/C&sub2; = C&sub3;/C&sub4;, no potential difference exists across the detector branch, yielding zero current.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Theoretical evaluation of balanced capacitance bridge networks.

solved_numericals.question: Three capacitors of capacitances 2 μF, 3 μF, and 6 μF are connected in series across a 100 V DC supply. Find the equivalent capacitance and the potential difference across the 3 μF capacitor.
solution_steps: Calculate total charge: Q = C_s * V = 1 μF * 100 V = 100 μC.
Calculate voltage across 3 μF capacitor: V&sub2; = Q / C&sub2; = 100 μC / 3 μF = 100/3 V.

solved_numericals.question: Two identical capacitors of capacitance C are connected in parallel and charged to a potential V. The DC source is disconnected, and a dielectric slab of dielectric constant K is inserted completely into one of the capacitors. Find the final common potential and the loss in electrostatic energy.
solution_steps: Initial total charge Q_total = CV + CV = 2CV. Initial total capacitance C_init = 2C.
After inserting dielectric, new capacitances are C and KC. Total new capacitance C_final = C(1 + K).
Since charge is conserved, final potential V_f = Q_total / C_final = 2CV / [C(1 + K)] = 2V / (1 + K).
Energy loss ΔU = U_i - U_f = CV^2 [1 - 2/(1 + K)] = CV^2 (K - 1)/(K + 1).

solved_numericals.question: Determine the equivalent capacitance of an infinite ladder network where each series branch has capacitance C&sub1; = 6 μF and each parallel shunt branch has capacitance C&sub2; = 3 μF connected across terminals AB.
solution_steps: Let the equivalent capacitance of the infinite network be C_eq.
Due to infinite repetition, removing the first unit cell leaves the remaining network with the same equivalent capacitance C_eq in parallel with C&sub2; and in series with C&sub1;.
Write the equation: C_eq = C_1 * (C_2 + C_eq) / [C_1 + C_2 + C_eq].
Substitute numerical values: C_eq = 6(3 + C_eq) / (6 + 3 + C_eq) = (18 + 6C_eq) / (9 + C_eq).
Form quadratic equation: C_eq(9 + C_eq) = 18 + 6C_eq ⇒ C_eq^2 + 3C_eq - 18 = 0.
Factorize: (C_eq + 6)(C_eq - 3) = 0. Reject negative capacitance, yielding C_eq = 3 μF.

assumptions_and_limitations: Capacitors are assumed to be ideal with zero leakage resistance and perfect dielectric isolation.
Connecting wires are treated as having zero resistance and negligible inductance, which fails under high-frequency transient or AC conditions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Connecting capacitors in series increases the total capacitance of the circuit.
common_misconceptions.correct: Connecting capacitors in series decreases the equivalent capacitance.
common_misconceptions.why: Series connection increases the effective plate separation distance, which is inversely proportional to capacitance.

common_misconceptions.wrong: When two capacitors of different values are connected in series, they store different magnitudes of charge.
common_misconceptions.correct: All capacitors connected in a single series branch store the exact same magnitude of charge.
common_misconceptions.why: Charge conservation on isolated inner plates dictates that equal and opposite charges are induced across series boundaries.

quick_revision: Series combination: 1/C_s = ∑ (1/C_i); equivalent capacitance is smaller than the smallest individual capacitor.
Parallel combination: C_p = ∑ C_i; equivalent capacitance is larger than the largest individual capacitor.
Energy conservation does not hold when charged capacitors are connected together; charge redistribution causes inherent energy dissipation.
